content: Between March 2016 and May 2017, several studies were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) care bundles in various settings, including high-income countries (HICs) like the United States and low-income countries (LICs) like Malawi and Niger. These studies aimed to assess the impact of structured interventions on maternal outcomes, including severe morbidity and mortality due to PPH. Below is a detailed summary of the findings: 1. United States (March 2016): A study involving 147 clusters and 9,821 women (vaginal or cesarean births) implemented the California Maternal Quality Care Collaborative (CMQCC) hemorrhage toolkit in 99 clusters (8,220 women). This toolkit included: Hemorrhage risk assessment. Active management of the third stage of labor. Emergency blood product release protocols. Usual care (48 clusters, 1,601 women) was not described. The study reported reduced rates of severe maternal morbidity but had a high risk of bias. 2. France (2002–2005): A before-and-after study in 19 maternity units with 35,386 women at risk of or experiencing PPH implemented a PPH protocol for 17,722 women. Key interventions included: Oxytocin administration during the third stage of labor for prevention. Use of blood collection bags after vaginal delivery for diagnosis. Treatments such as manual removal of the placenta, uterine cavity examination, intravenous oxytocin, sulprostone for persistent PPH, and red blood cell transfusion for hematocrit <28%. Usual care (17,664 women) lacked national clinical guidelines. The study reported increased rates of transfusion and hemostatic surgery but insufficient data on other critical outcomes. 3. United States (May 2013–October 2016): A study across 58 hospitals with 2,852 health workers implemented the AWHONN (Association of Women’s Health, Obstetric, and Neonatal Nurses) PPH bundle. This included: Updated obstetric hemorrhage policies and staff education. Blood loss quantification at birth. Risk assessments at admission, before, and after birth. Debriefing after hemorrhages. The study reported insufficient data on critical outcomes and a high risk of bias. 4. Malawi (March 2016–May 2017): A study in a central hospital and district health center with 2,694 women implemented a hemorrhage bundle for 1,045 women. This included: Blood loss quantification and risk assessment tools. Active management of the third stage of labor. Standardized hemorrhage protocols and checklists. Simulation training and communication protocols. Usual care (890 women) was associated with higher maternal mortality rates. The bundle reduced maternal mortality from bleeding but lacked sufficient data on other outcomes. 5. United States (June 2018–June 2020): A quality improvement initiative involving 13,659 women (4,912 receiving the intervention) included: Hemorrhage risk assessment. Education on protocols, unit-based drills, and post-drill debriefs. Active management of the third stage of labor. Multidisciplinary reviews of severe hemorrhages. Usual care (8,747 women) showed higher rates of severe maternal morbidity. The intervention reduced severe morbidity and transfusion rates but lacked data on other outcomes. 6. United States (April 2014–December 2018): A study with 2,297 women implemented the AWHONN PPH bundle for 1,244 women. This included: Hemorrhage carts with medications and supplies. Massive transfusion protocols and response teams. Active management of the third stage of labor. Automated blood loss quantification. Stage-based intervention recommendations and debriefing. Usual care (1,053 women) had a higher risk of adverse outcomes. The study reported insufficient data on critical outcomes. 7. Niger (November 2012–December 2020): A study across 8 regional hospitals, 35 district centers, and 1,217 peripheral health centers with 435,336 women implemented a PPH bundle for 343,668 women. This included: Misoprostol for prevention and treatment. Intrauterine condom tamponade and anti-shock garments. Public health organizational tools. Usual care (91,668 women) showed higher maternal mortality rates. The bundle reduced all-cause maternal mortality and mortality from bleeding. 8. United States (January 2017–May 2020): A study in 9 hospitals with 18,520 women implemented an obstetric hemorrhage bundle for 9,248 women. This included: Risk assessment and immediate availability of supplies. Education, drills, checklists, and response algorithms. Feedback mechanisms, interdisciplinary reviews, and debriefings. Usual care (9,272 women) showed higher rates of severe PPH (≥1,000 mL). The bundle reduced severe PPH rates but lacked data on other outcomes. 9. United States (October 2017–December 2019): A study with 6,735 women implemented the CMQCC Obstetric Hemorrhage Toolkit for 3,425 women. This included: PPH risk assessment and blood loss quantification. Uterotonics for blood loss ≥500 mL (vaginal delivery) or ≥1,000 mL (cesarean). Tranexamic acid for blood loss ≥1,000 mL. Activation of a PPH code for blood loss ≥1,500 mL. Usual care (3,310 women) showed higher rates of severe PPH. The study reported insufficient data on other outcomes. In summary, these studies highlight the effectiveness of structured PPH care bundles in reducing maternal morbidity and mortality. However, many studies were limited by high risks of bias and insufficient data on critical outcomes.
